source: CARDI book "ដំណាំស្រូវនៅកម្ពុជា" (Rice Cultivation in Cambodia), by Men Sarom, Thuy Lina and Pheng Thimuny, published by CARDI, 2007, Chapter 8 (Fertilizer and nutrient management), sections 8.3.9 (Aluminum toxicity) and 8.3.10 (Acid sulfate soil / iron toxicity). No elibrary URL visible.
text: Aluminum (Al) toxicity occurs in acidic soils where low pH releases aluminum into the soil solution as Al3+, which is directly toxic to rice roots (causing stubby, thickened, poorly-branched roots and stunted plant growth) and also interferes with uptake of calcium (Ca2+) and magnesium (Mg2+) because Al3+ competes for the same uptake pathways, and disturbs root-level plant hormone (phytohormone) activity. The source describes Al3+ solubility rising sharply once soil water pH drops below about 5.0, with clay content also playing a role (soils with less than roughly 30% clay reach damaging Al3+ concentrations more easily); at pH 4.0 or below, both H+ and Al3+ become highly mobile and damaging (Seng, 2000). Visible symptoms include a stubby 'brush-like' root system, stunted and dark-green foliage, poor tillering, and general nutrient-deficiency symptoms (especially phosphorus and magnesium) even when those nutrients are present in the soil, because Al3+ blocks their uptake. Recommended remediation: apply agricultural lime (CaCO3) to raise soil pH, which both directly reduces Al3+ solubility and supplies competing Ca2+ ions that displace Al3+ from root-uptake sites (Seng et al., 2006); the source notes that soils high in sulfate (SO4 2-) or nitrate (NO3-) anions release Ca2+ from applied lime more readily than soils dominated by chloride (Cl-), which can slow the liming response. A related but distinct soil-constraint problem covered alongside Al toxicity is acid sulfate soil, where drainage of naturally sulfur-rich soils exposes iron pyrite/iron sulfide minerals (FeS, and hydrogen sulfide gas H2S) in the root zone (rhizosphere) to oxygen, generating sulfuric acid and releasing high levels of ferrous iron (Fe2+); this excess Fe2+ similarly blocks phosphorus, calcium, magnesium, and potassium uptake, and soils containing kaolinite clay are noted as particularly prone to this problem. Diagnostic and management approaches for acid sulfate soil mirror those for general iron toxicity/bronzing (already covered elsewhere in this knowledge base): maintain shallow standing water rather than letting the field dry and re-oxidize, avoid disturbing the subsoil layer where pyrite is concentrated, and apply lime and balanced P/K fertilization to counteract nutrient lockout.
caveat: This source names aluminum toxicity as a distinct soil-management topic from the salinity and iron-toxicity/bronzing content already in the knowledge base (from earlier batches) - recommend a duplicate-check against existing soil-constraint entries once repo access is available, since some overlap with the existing iron toxicity/bronzing entry is likely, particularly for the acid sulfate soil portion. Dense supporting tables in this section of the source (e.g. a named 'table 8.7' referenced for soil groups susceptible to Al toxicity) were not transcribed due to the same dense-table reading difficulty noted elsewhere in this project - only the clearly-legible prose mechanisms and remediation guidance are included here.
